questions.q: What is a shell?
options: A program whose primary purpose is to read commands and run other programs
The physical case of a computer
questions.explain: The shell is the command-line interface between you and the operating system.
questions.evidence: A shell is a program whose primary purpose is to read commands and run other programs.

questions.q: What does a command-line interface (CLI) let users do?
options: Interact with a computer by reading and writing text
questions.explain: Text commands are easy to repeat, combine and automate.
questions.evidence: A command-line interface (CLI) allows users to interact with a computer by reading and writing text.

questions.q: What is your current working directory?
options: The one place you are in at any moment while using the shell
The folder where the shell program is installed
The root of the file system
questions.explain: Relative paths are interpreted from the current working directory (see pwd).
questions.evidence: at any time while we are using the shell, we are in exactly one place called our current working directory

questions.q: Why is it better to avoid spaces in the names of files and directories?
options: Spaces are not allowed by any operating system
Spaces are used to separate arguments on the command line
questions.explain: Use hyphens or underscores instead, e.g. north-pacific-gyre.
questions.evidence: since spaces are used to separate arguments on the command line it is better to avoid them in names of files and directories.

questions.q: A command is waiting for input and seems stuck. How do you get out?
questions.explain: Ctrl + C interrupts the running program.
questions.evidence: you can escape out of this state by holding down the control key ( Ctrl ) and pressing the letter C once

questions.q: What do loops let you do in the shell?
options: Repeat a command or set of commands for each item in a list
questions.explain: for filename in *.dat; do …; done applies the same steps to every file.
questions.evidence: Loops are a programming construct which allow us to repeat a command or set of commands for each item in a list.

questions.q: What is a shell script?
options: A set of commands saved in a file — really a small program
A log of commands you typed yesterday
questions.explain: Saving repeated commands lets you re-run a whole workflow with a single command.
questions.evidence: a bunch of commands saved in a file is usually called a shell script

questions.q: Which command finds files and directories whose names match simple patterns?
questions.explain: grep searches inside files for lines that match; find searches for the files themselves.
questions.evidence: Use find to find files and directories whose names match simple patterns.

questions.q: When is UDP a suitable protocol?
options: When every packet must arrive in order
When speed and efficiency matter more than guaranteed delivery
questions.explain: Streaming, gaming and DNS lookups prefer speed; TCP guarantees delivery.
questions.evidence: UDP is suitable for applications where speed and efficiency are more important than guaranteed delivery

questions.q: Why is network segmentation used?
options: To reduce the number of IP addresses
To make the network easier to cable
To contain the impact of breaches and limit attackers' lateral movement
questions.explain: Isolated segments with strict access policies stop an intruder spreading.
questions.evidence: Network segmentation is used to improve security by containing the impact of potential breaches and limiting lateral movement for attackers within the network.

questions.q: What does the HTTPS guidance require for your service, including its APIs?
options: It must only be accessible through secure connections
It must allow plain HTTP for older browsers
It must use a separate domain for each page
It must block all mobile devices
questions.explain: Encryption in transit stops information being intercepted or modified.
questions.evidence: you must make sure your service (including APIs ) is only accessible through secure connections.

questions.q: Which part of the operating system manages files and directories?
questions.explain: The shell is one way of interacting with it.
questions.evidence: The part of the operating system responsible for managing files and directories is called the file system

questions.q: What does the command pwd stand for?
questions.explain: It shows where you are in the file system.
questions.evidence: running a command called pwd (which stands for 'print working directory')

questions.q: How is an absolute path written?
options: As the full path from the root directory, starting with a slash
questions.explain: Relative paths start from your current working directory instead.
questions.evidence: it is possible to specify the absolute path to a directory by including its entire path from the root directory, which is indicated by a leading slash

questions.q: What does ls -t do?
options: Lists items by time of last change instead of alphabetically
questions.explain: ls has many options, and you can combine them.
questions.evidence: The command ls -t lists items by time of last change instead of alphabetically.

questions.q: What is the difference between cd .. and cd -?
options: cd .. goes up one level; cd - goes back to the previous directory
They do exactly the same thing
questions.explain: Up means the parent directory; back means where you were before.
questions.evidence: the former brings you up

questions.q: Are the files you see in the shell different from those in a file explorer?
options: Yes, the shell has its own copies
No — they are the same files, accessed in two ways
questions.explain: Changes in one show up in the other.
questions.evidence: While the shell and the file explorer are two different ways of interacting with the files, the files and directories themselves are the same.

questions.q: Does mv ask before overwriting an existing file?
questions.explain: Be careful: mv can silently replace a file.
questions.evidence: By default, mv will not ask for confirmation before overwriting files.

questions.q: Can files deleted with rm always be recovered?
options: No — there's no guarantee, as the disk space may be reused immediately
questions.explain: The shell has no recycle bin.
questions.evidence: since the computer may recycle the file's disk space right away

questions.q: What does rm -i do?
options: Asks for confirmation before every removal
questions.explain: It's a safer way to delete files.
questions.evidence: The -i option will prompt before (every) removal

questions.q: When you use wildcards such as *.txt, what do commands like ls actually receive?
options: The list of matching file names, not the wildcard itself
questions.explain: The shell expands wildcards before running the command.
questions.evidence: commands like wc and ls see the lists of file names matching these expressions, but not the wildcards themselves

questions.q: Why does wc -l *.pdb > lengths.txt print nothing on screen?
options: Its output was redirected into lengths.txt
questions.explain: > sends output to a file instead of the screen.
questions.evidence: This command prints no screen output, because everything that wc would have printed has gone into the file lengths.txt instead.

questions.q: What does sort -n do?
questions.explain: Without -n, 10 sorts before 2.
questions.evidence: The -n option specifies a numerical rather than an alphanumerical sort.

questions.q: Is it safe to redirect a command's output into the same file it is reading?
options: No — it's a very bad idea
questions.explain: The file can be emptied before the command reads it.
questions.evidence: It's a very bad idea to try redirecting the output of a command that operates on a file to the same file.

questions.q: What problem do pipes solve compared with saving intermediate files?
options: Intermediate files make it hard to follow what's going on
questions.explain: A pipe sends one command's output straight into the next.
questions.evidence: those intermediate files make it hard to follow what's going on

questions.q: What is each run of a loop called?
questions.explain: Each iteration assigns the next item in the list to the loop variable.
questions.evidence: Each time the loop runs (called an iteration)

questions.q: In a shell for loop, which word marks the end of the loop?
questions.explain: The word do marks the start of the commands to repeat.
questions.evidence: The word "done" indicates the end of a loop

questions.q: How do you loop over file names that contain spaces?
options: Put quotes around them and around the loop variable
Use a backslash at the end of the line
questions.explain: Spaces otherwise split one name into two items.
questions.evidence: If one of those elements contains a space character, we need to surround it with quotes, and do the same thing to our loop variable.

questions.q: How do you use the value of a loop variable inside the loop?
options: Prefix its name with a dollar sign
questions.explain: Without $, the shell treats it as plain text.
questions.evidence: expanding the loop variable name because we have prefixed it with a dollar sign

questions.q: When editing shell scripts, which kind of editor should you use?
options: A plain text editor, or save files as plain text
questions.explain: Word processors add formatting characters that break scripts.
questions.evidence: When editing programs, therefore, you must either use a plain text editor or be careful to save files as plain text.

questions.q: Why save frequently repeated commands in a file?
options: So you can re-run them all later with a single command
To hide them from other users
questions.explain: Such a file is a shell script — a small program.
questions.evidence: We are going to take the commands we repeat frequently and save them in files so that we can re-run all those operations again later by typing a single command.

questions.q: Inside a shell script, what does $1 mean?
options: The first filename or other argument on the command line
The first line of the file
questions.explain: It makes scripts work on any file you pass in.
questions.evidence: means 'the first filename (or other argument) on the command line'

questions.q: What does the special variable $@ mean in a script?
options: All the command-line arguments passed to the script
questions.explain: Put it in double quotes to handle names with spaces.
questions.evidence: which means, 'All of the command-line arguments to the shell script'

questions.q: What does grep do?
options: Finds and prints lines in files that match a pattern
questions.explain: find, by contrast, finds files and directories.
questions.evidence: grep finds and prints lines in files that match a pattern

questions.q: Searching for 'The' also matched the word 'Thesis'. Why?
options: grep matches the pattern inside larger words unless told otherwise
questions.explain: Options can restrict matches to whole words.
questions.evidence: one of which contained our search pattern within a larger word, 'Thesis'

questions.q: Which grep option limits matches to whole words?
questions.explain: -n numbers matching lines; -i ignores case.
questions.evidence: we can give grep the -w option

questions.q: Which grep option makes a search case-insensitive?
questions.explain: Then 'The' and 'the' both match.
questions.evidence: use the option -i to make our search case-insensitive

questions.q: When is TCP the right protocol?
options: When speed matters more than delivery
When applications need reliable, ordered delivery and accurate data
questions.explain: UDP suits streaming and gaming, where speed matters more than guaranteed delivery.
questions.evidence: TCP prioritizes reliability and ordered delivery, making it suitable for applications that require data accuracy

questions.q: How does network segmentation support identity-based access control?
options: It removes the need for logins
Users and devices are authenticated and authorised before reaching specific segments
It gives every user full access
questions.explain: Access between segments follows security policies.
questions.evidence: Network segmentation also aids in enforcing identity-based access controls, where users and devices are thoroughly authenticated and authorized before accessing specific segments.

questions.q: What do cloud security groups let organisations define?
options: Rules for which types of traffic are allowed and denied
questions.explain: They add a layer of defence to cloud deployments.
questions.evidence: Security groups allow organizations to define rules that determine which types of traffic are allowed and denied
